opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it's one of the things that drew me here. In a lot of places I've worked, the biggest barrier to doing meaningful work with health data wasn't the algorithms. It was the data itself. You'd have a patient whose records were scattered across three or four hospital systems that didn't talk to each other, each with its own formats and coding conventions. You'd spend most of a project just stitching things together and cleaning them up, and you'd still end up with gaps.

Having a single, province-wide system like Connect Care changes that equation quite a bit. You have a much more complete longitudinal picture of a patient: their visits, labs, imaging, medications, and outcomes, all in a consistent structure across a population of over four million people. For someone like me who's interested in things like predicting how a patient's disease will progress, or how they'll respond to a particular treatment, that continuity is enormously valuable. You can't model a trajectory well if you only see pieces of it.

It also matters for generalizability. A model trained at one academic hospital often doesn't hold up when you move it to a rural clinic or a different patient population. With province-wide data you can build and validate across that diversity from the start.

That said, I don't want to oversell it. A unified system doesn't automatically mean clean or research-ready data. EHRs are built for clinical care and billing, not for machine learning, so there's still a lot of work in understanding how data gets entered, what's missing and why, and what biases are baked in. And access has to be handled carefully. The privacy, governance, and trust pieces are just as important as the technical ones. Patients need confidence that their data is being used responsibly and for their benefit.

But as a foundation, it's a real opportunity. It puts Alberta in a position to do things that would be very hard to do almost anywhere else, and to move from research findings to tools that actually get back into the clinic.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a single province-wide system improves access to a more complete, consistent longitudinal patient record, making health-data research easier.

r002.rationale: The candidate says nothing about Ontario, a failed common-record effort, or the eHealth scandal.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, Connect Care is one of the things that drew me here. When I was doing imaging and AI work before, so much of the effort went into just stitching data together: one hospital on one system, the clinic down the road on another, radiology reports in a different format from pathology. You'd spend eighty percent of a project on plumbing before you asked a single scientific question.

What Alberta has done with a single provincial Epic instance is remove a lot of that plumbing problem up front. Every patient in the province, from a rural clinic to a tertiary centre in Edmonton or Calgary, is in one record with one data model. For someone building predictive models, that's rare. It means longitudinal data, so I can follow a patient through diagnosis, treatment, and years of follow-up rather than seeing a snapshot. It means the imaging, the labs, the medications, and the clinical notes are actually linked instead of being matched up after the fact. And it means the population is representative, not just whoever happened to show up at an academic hospital.

The other piece I'm excited about is the deployment side. Building a model is the easy part. Getting it in front of a clinician in a way that changes a decision is where most AI in healthcare dies. If your model can plug into the same system every clinician in the province is already looking at, you have a path from research to practice that most jurisdictions simply don't have.

I'd add two caveats. One system doesn't automatically mean clean data; the data still reflects how busy people document under pressure, so a lot of the work is understanding what a field really means. And having everything in one place raises the stakes on governance and privacy, so we need to earn that trust with Albertans and do this carefully. But as a starting point for learning from health data at scale, I think Alberta is in a position very few places in the world are.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Alberta’s single provincial Epic instance removes data-stitching work and links longitudinal records, making data easier to use for research and deployment.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Ontario or attribute the collapse of a common-record effort to the eHealth scandal.

astra-6.text:
A province-wide system creates an opportunity to connect information that would otherwise be scattered across hospitals and clinics. You can start to follow a patient’s journey over time, rather than seeing only one encounter. For research and AI, that could help us understand patterns in care and identify where we might improve outcomes.

But having a common medical record system is only part of the work. We still need to understand how the data were collected, where information is missing, and whether the patients represented reflect the people we want to help. And we need responsible ways to access and use those data that protect privacy and maintain patients’ trust. The opportunity is to turn that infrastructure into better care.

r001.rationale: It says a province-wide system can connect information otherwise scattered across hospitals and clinics, making patient data easier to use over time.

r002.rationale: It does not mention Ontario’s effort or tentatively link its collapse to the eHealth scandal.

sol-6.1.text: I see it as a tremendous opportunity. Having a province-wide medical record system gives us a more consistent view of a patient’s journey through the health system, rather than having pieces of that story scattered across different institutions. That creates a foundation for asking better research questions and developing AI tools that could improve care. But having the system is only the starting point. We still need to understand the quality of the data, make it accessible for appropriate research, and ensure that we’re protecting patients’ privacy.

r001.rationale: The response says a province-wide medical record gives a more consistent view of a patient’s journey and creates a foundation for research and AI, making patient data easier to use.
